claims.source: This background recombination labels 3–11 neurons/DRG (5.2 ± 1.6 neurons/DRG, n = 47 DRGs from three animals) in 3–4 pw animals (Figure 2C), which represents <1% of the total Mrgprd+ nociceptor population (Zylka et al., 2005; Wright et al., 1997; Molliver et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is calculated based on the number of labeled neurons and supported by citations to Zylka et al. 2005, Wright et al. 1997, and Molliver et al. 1997.

claims.claim: Sparsely labeled DRG neurons in untreated MrgprdCreERT2; RosaiAP mice co-express non-peptidergic nociceptor markers peripherin, PAP, and RET.
claims.source: The sparsely labeled DRG neurons co-express non-peptidergic nociceptor markers peripherin, PAP (Zylka et al., 2008), and RET (Figure 2D,F,H)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 2D, F, and H.

claims.claim: Sparsely labeled DRG neurons in untreated MrgprdCreERT2; RosaiAP mice do not express NF200 or CGRP.
claims.source: The sparsely labeled DRG neurons co-express non-peptidergic nociceptor markers peripherin, PAP (Zylka et al., 2008), and RET (Figure 2D,F,H), but do not express NF200 or CGRP (Figure 2E,G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 2E and G.

claims.claim: 93.7 ± 2.3% of AP+ neurons in untreated MrgprdCreERT2/EGFPf; RosaiAP mice co-express MrgprdEGFPf.
claims.source: We generated MrgprdCreERT2/EGFPf; RosaiAP triple mice and found that almost all AP+ neurons co-express MrgprdEGFPf (93. 7 ± 2.3%, n = 126 AP+ neurons from three animals) (Figure 2I) in 3 to 4pw mice.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: 98.4% (130/132 arbors, n = 4 animals) of single-cell arbors have a 'bushy ending' morphology.
claims.source: We found that 98.4% (130/132 arbors, n = 4 animals) of single-cell arbors have a 'bushy ending' morphology (Figure 3A and B,D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Wu et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining of skin in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and supported by citation to Wu et al. 2012.

claims.claim: Arbors in glabrous plantar paw skin have single, un-branched thickened neurites at their distal ends.
claims.source: The distal ends of arbors in glabrous plantar paw skin have single, un-branched thickened neurites (Figure 3A and B)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining of plantar paw skin in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: Arbors in hairy skin feature both un-branched neurites as well as dense neurite clusters.
claims.source: while arbors in the hairy skin feature both un-branched neurites as well as dense neurite clusters (Figure 3D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining of hairy skin in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: Dense neurite clusters in hairy skin form circumferential-like endings that innervate the necks of hair follicles.
claims.source: These dense clusters form circumferential-like endings that innervate the necks of hair follicles (red arrowheads in Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Zylka et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining in Figure 3E and F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and supported by citation to Zylka et al. 2005.

claims.claim: All three types of hair follicles in mouse hairy skin (guard, awl/auchenne, and zigzag) are innervated by MrgprdEGFPf fibers.
claims.source: Whole mount immunostaining of MrgprdEGFPf skin shows that all three types of hair follicles in mouse hairy skin (guard, awl/auchenne, and zigzag [Li et al., 2011]) are innervated by MrgprdEGFPf fibers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-H and supported by citation to Li et al. 2011.

claims.claim: 1.6% of arbors in hairy skin have 'free endings' lacking thickened structures.
claims.source: A very small minority (1.6%) of arbors in the hairy skin have "free endings" (Wu et al., 2012) lacking these thickened structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C and supported by citation to Wu et al. 2012.

claims.claim: Mrgprd+ neuron density is higher in the proximal hind limb (97.6 ± 33.4 cells/mm2) compared to plantar paw (21.0 ± 3.0 cells/mm2).
claims.source: Consistent with the overall neurite density, we found that the neuron density is higher in the proximal hind limb compared to plantar paw (cells/mm2 of skin: proximal hind limb = 97.6 ± 33.4, plantar hind paw = 21.0 ± 3.0, n = 7 injections for each, p=0.04, Student's t test) (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by retrograde DiI labeling data in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Most Mrgprd+ central branches do not bifurcate (65.8%, n = 234 neurons from 3 animals).
claims.source: Most Mrgprd+ central branches do not bifurcate (65.8%, n = 234 neurons from 3 animals), and most also terminate within the segment of entry (72.6%) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining of spinal cord and quantified in Table 1.

claims.claim: Most Mrgprd+ central branches terminate within the segment of entry (72.6%).
claims.source: Most Mrgprd+ central branches do not bifurcate (65.8%, n = 234 neurons from 3 animals), and most also terminate within the segment of entry (72.6%) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining of spinal cord and quantified in Table 1.

claims.claim: 34.2% of Mrgprd+ central branches bifurcate one or more times in the spinal cord.
claims.source: However, some (34.2%) bifurcate one or more times in the spinal cord, and some (27.3%) travel up to 3 segments from the point of entry (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining of spinal cord and quantified in Table 1.

claims.claim: 27.3% of Mrgprd+ central branches travel up to 3 segments from the point of entry.
claims.source: However, some (34.2%) bifurcate one or more times in the spinal cord, and some (27.3%) travel up to 3 segments from the point of entry (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining of spinal cord and quantified in Table 1.

claims.claim: 91.9% of labeled nociceptors have only one arbor.
claims.source: The majority (91.9%) of labeled nociceptors have only one arbor, but a few have 2 (6.8%), or 3 (0.9%) central arbors, and for a small number of Mrgprd + nociceptors (0.4%), we could not identify any arbor (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining of spinal cord and quantified in Table 1.

claims.claim: Mrgprd+ non-peptidergic nociceptor central arbors display two different morphologies that can be distinguished by the ratio of their mediolateral width to their rostrocaudal height (W/H ratio).
claims.source: Strikingly, Mrgprd+ non-peptidergic nociceptor central arbors display two different morphologies that can be distinguished by the ratio of their mediolateral width to their rostrocaudal height (W/H ratio) (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining and measurements in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Arbors with W/H ratios > 0.2 are defined as 'round'.
claims.source: We defined arbors with W/H ratios > 0.2 as 'round' (Figure 4A–C,H, and Figure 4—source data 1)
claims.evidence: This is a definition established by the authors based on morphological measurements.

claims.claim: Arbors with W/H ratios < 0.2 are defined as 'long and thin'.
claims.source: and arbors with W/H ratios < 0.2 as 'long and thin' (Figure 4B–F,H, and Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a definition established by the authors based on morphological measurements.

claims.claim: Round arbors are found in DH regions known to represent the distal limbs, tail, anogenital, and head/face skin.
claims.source: Further, these morphological types are regionally segregated. Round arbors are found in DH regions known to represent the distal limbs (medial cervical and lumbar enlargements) as well as tail, anogenital (sacral DH), and head/face (descending trigeminal terminals in the upper cervical DH and medulla) skin (Figure 4B and C,H,J, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) (Koerber and Brown, 1982; Molander and Grant, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining in Figure 4 and supported by citations to Koerber and Brown 1982 and Molander and Grant 1985.

claims.claim: Long arbors are located in regions corresponding to the proximal limbs and trunk skin.
claims.source: Long arbors are instead located in regions corresponding to the proximal limbs (lateral cervical and lumbar enlargements) and trunk skin (thoracic DH) (Figure 4B–F,H,J) (Koerber and Brown, 1982; Molander and Grant, 1985; Cervero and Connell, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining in Figure 4 and supported by citations to Koerber and Brown 1982, Molander and Grant 1985, and Cervero and Connell 1984.

claims.claim: Round and long arbors do not differ in area.
claims.source: While round and long arbors differ in morphology, they do not differ in area (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by area measurements in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The number of labeled peripheral arbors in the toe and plantar paw skin shows a very close correlation with the number of round DH terminals in the corresponding half of the lumbar enlargement.
claims.source: We compared the number of labeled peripheral arbors in the toe and plantar paw skin with the number of round DH terminals in the corresponding half of the lumbar enlargement. This showed a very close correlation (Figure 4I)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Round central arbors of the lumbar enlargement correspond to plantar paw and digit Mrgprd+ nociceptors.
claims.source: supporting that the round central arbors of the lumbar enlargement correspond to plantar paw and digit Mrgprd+ nociceptors, while nociceptors from other regions of the hindlimb (including dorsal hindpaw and proximal hindlimb) grow long central arbors located more laterally.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation data in Figure 4I and somatotopic mapping literature.

claims.claim: Long and round arbor types occupy mutually exclusive zones of the DH despite increased labeling density.
claims.source: Using increasing dosages of tamoxifen, we found that these arbor types occupy mutually exclusive zones of the DH (Figure 5). The maintained segregation of long and round arbors in the DH despite the increased number of AP+ DRG neurons indicates that these arbor morphologies represent a true somatotopic distinction among Mrgprd+ non-peptidergic nociceptors.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AP staining with increasing tamoxifen doses in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Peripheral arbors of neighboring non-peptidergic nociceptors do not tile but instead overlap extensively.
claims.source: The arbor fields of individual double tdT+/EGFP+ neurons are always co-innervated by EGFP-only+ fibers in both hairy and glabrous skin (Figure 6A–D), indicating that peripheral arbors of neighboring non-peptidergic nociceptors do not tile but instead overlap extensively.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining of MrgprdCreERT2/EGFPf; RosatdTomato skin in Figure 6A-D.

claims.claim: Multiple Mrgprd+ neurons can innervate a single hair follicle.
claims.source: In hairy skin, sparse labeled tdT+ neurites co-innervated hair follicles with EGFP-only+ fibers, indicating that multiple Mrgprd+ neurons can innervate a single hair follicle.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining of MrgprdCreERT2/EGFPf; RosatdTomato hairy skin in Figure 6A-C.

claims.claim: Both round and long DH arbors of non-peptidergic nociceptors highly overlap with their neighbors in the DH.
claims.source: Similarly, both round and long DH arbors of non-peptidergic nociceptors highly overlap with their neighbors in the DH (Figure 6E and F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining of spinal cord sections in Figure 6E and F.

claims.claim: Comparable expression of ChR2-EYFP was found for Mrgprd+ neurons in thoracic (T9-T12) and hind limb-level (L3-L5) DRGs.
claims.source: Comparable expression of ChR2-EYFP, as measured by the native fluorescence intensity, was found for Mrgprd+ neurons in thoracic (T9-T12) and hind limb-level (L3-L5) DRGs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence measurements in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claims.claim: In MrgprdCreERT2/+; RosaChR2-EYFP/ChR2-EYFP homozygous mice, 82.4% (14/17) of medial lumbar DH neurons show monosynaptic EPSCLs.
claims.source: Almost all recorded neurons in both medial and lateral lumbar DH showed EPSCLs (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 1), with most cells (14/17 = 82.4% in medial lumbar, 14/16 = 86.5% in lateral lumbar) showing monosynaptic EPSCLs in both locations.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: In MrgprdCreERT2/+; RosaChR2-EYFP/ChR2-EYFP homozygous mice, 86.5% (14/16) of lateral lumbar DH neurons show monosynaptic EPSCLs.
claims.source: Almost all recorded neurons in both medial and lateral lumbar DH showed EPSCLs (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 1), with most cells (14/17 = 82.4% in medial lumbar, 14/16 = 86.5% in lateral lumbar) showing monosynaptic EPSCLs in both locations.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The incidence of receiving direct Mrgprd+ input is equivalent for medial lumbar and lateral lumbar DH in ChR2 homozygous mice.
claims.source: This indicates that the majority of DH neurons in this innervation territory receive direct Mrgprd+ input, and that the incidence receiving direct input is equivalent for medial lumbar and lateral lumbar DH.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data in Figure 7D showing similar response incidences.

claims.claim: RosaChR2-EYFP heterozygous DRGs have a ~40% reduction in ChR2-EYFP protein compared to RosaChR2-EYFP homozygous DRGs.
claims.source: RosaChR2-EYFP hetereozygous DRGs have a ~ 40% reduction in ChR2-EYFP protein compared to RosaChR2-EYFP homozygous DRGs based on Western blotting (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E.

claims.claim: In ChR2 heterozygous mice, medial lumbar DH neurons showed a ~9 fold higher (88.2% vs. 10.5%) incidence of monosynaptic EPSCLs compared to lateral lumbar neurons.
claims.source: Medial lumbar DH neurons showed a much higher incidence of light responses than lateral lumbar neurons, with a ~ 9 fold higher (15/17 = 88.2% vs. 2/19 = 10.5%) incidence of monosynaptic EPSCLs over lateral lumbar neurons (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: The incidence of monosynaptic EPSCLs in medial and lateral thoracic DH neurons is 9.1% (1/11) in ChR2 heterozygous mice.
claims.source: Similar to the lateral lumbar DH, the incidence of monosynaptic EPSCLs of layer II neurons in the medial and lateral thoracic region are also very low (1/11 = 9.1%) (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: The pulse duration threshold required to elicit EPSCLs was much longer in lateral lumbar and thoracic DH neurons compared to medial lumbar neurons.
claims.source: Moreover, even among responsive neurons, the pulse duration threshold required to elicit EPSCLs was much longer in lateral lumbar and thoracic DH neurons compared to medial lumbar neurons (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Upper leg skin shows a much higher density of EYFP+ neurites than the paw glabrous skin.
claims.source: Consistent with the AP labeling (Figure 3), upper leg skin shows a much higher density of EYFP+ neurites than the paw glabrous skin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C.

claims.claim: ChR2-EYFP+ neurites in paw glabrous skin terminate much farther from the surface than leg hairy skin neurites.
claims.source: In addition, ChR2-EYFP+ neurites in paw glabrous skin terminate much farther from the surface than leg hairy skin neurites (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B,D) due to the thicker outer stratum corneum layer in glabrous skin.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and measurements in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B, and D.

claims.claim: Green light (5 mW, 10 Hz, sine wave) stimulation of paw skin does not induce avoidance behavior in control or MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFP mice.
claims.source: We first stimulated the paw skin of both groups of mice with green light (5 mW, 10 Hz, sine wave) and observed no avoidance behavior such as paw withdrawal (Figure 8C, Videos 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 8C and Videos 1 and 2.

claims.claim: 1 mW blue light stimulation of paw skin induces paw withdrawal in 12.5% of MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFP mice but not in control mice.
claims.source: When we stimulated both groups of mice with 1 mW of blue light (10 Hz, sine wave), control mice did not respond, while 12.5% of MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFP mice displayed light-induced paw withdrawal (Figure 8B and C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: 5 mW blue light stimulation of paw skin induces paw withdrawal in 100% of MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFP mice but not in control mice.
claims.source: When stimulated with 5 mW blue light (10 Hz, sine wave), 100% of MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFP mice displayed clear light-induced paw withdrawal. Control mice still did not respond (Figure 8B and C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, Videos 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 8C and Videos 3 and 4.

claims.claim: 5 mW blue light stimulation of upper-thigh skin does not induce avoidance behavior in control or MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFP mice.
claims.source: Strikingly, when we activated Mrgprd+ neurites in the shaved upper-thigh skin, neither control nor MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFP mice responded to 5 mW blue light (Figure 8E and F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, Videos 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 8F and Videos 5 and 6.

claims.claim: 10 or 20 mW blue light is required to observe a fully penetrant avoidance behavior response in the upper-thigh of MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFP mice.
claims.source: Rather, to observe a fully penetrant avoidance behavior response in the upper-thigh of MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFPmice, the blue light power intensity had to be increased to 10 or 20 mW (2–4 times higher than the requirement in the paw) (Figure 8E–G, Videos 7 and 8).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 8F and G and Videos 7 and 8.

claims.claim: 20 mW intensity blue light is required at the leg to trigger responses comparable to 5 mW intensity stimulation of the paw when considering temporal delay of avoidance responses.
claims.source: When taking the temporal delay of avoidance responses (Figure 8H) into consideration, 20 mW intensity blue light is required at the leg to trigger responses comparable to 5 mW intensity stimulation of the paw.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 8H.

claims.claim: The light intensity threshold required to trigger an avoidance response is significantly lower in the paw compared to the upper-limb of MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFP mice.
claims.source: In short, the light intensity threshold required to trigger an avoidance response is significantly lower in the paw compared to the upper-limb of MrgprdCreERT2; RosaChR2-EYFPmice.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral data in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The wider mediolateral spread of plantar paw nociceptor central arbors could facilitate 'afferent magnification' in downstream CNS circuits.
claims.source: In this study, we identified a novel somatotopic organization in the central arbors of mammalian Mrgprd+ nociceptors, which is very well correlated with a regional increase in the sensitivity of paw nociceptive circuits to external stimuli. Our results suggest a model (Figure 8I), in which the wider mediolateral spread of plantar paw nociceptor central arbors could facilitate 'afferent magnification" (Catania and Kaas, 1997) in downstream CNS circuits and facilitate heightened pain sensitivity of the plantar paw.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed by the authors based on their data and supported by citation to Catania and Kaas 1997.

claims.claim: Two features of mouse non-peptidergic nociceptors (peripheral neurite density distribution and heightened sensitivity of pain processing in the distal limb) are consistent with findings in humans.
claims.source: Remarkably, two features of mouse non-peptidergic nociceptors revealed by our study, the peripheral neurite density distribution and the heightened sensitivity of pain processing in the distal limb, are consistent with findings in humans (Mancini et al., 2012; Mancini et al., 2013; Mancini et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's findings and previous human studies, supported by citations to Mancini et al.

claims.claim: The organizational mechanisms discovered in mice are likely to be conserved in humans.
claims.source: Therefore, the organizational mechanisms we discovered in mice are likely to be conserved in humans, which provides a possible explanation for the human 'pain fovea'.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the consistency between mouse and human findings.

claims.claim: Adult mice have two functionally distinct DRG neuronal populations expressing Mas-related gene product receptor (Mrgpr) genes.
claims.source: Adult mice have two functionally distinct DRG neuronal populations expressing Mas-related gene product receptor (Mrgpr) genes. One expresses Mrgpra, Mrgprb, and Mrgprc genes and the other only expresses Mrgprd (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2008; Dong et al., 2001; Han et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2007; Zylka et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Mrgpra/b/c+ neurons transiently express Mrgprd during early development.
claims.source: Mrgpra/b/c+ neurons also transiently express Mrgprd during early development (Liu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al. 2008.

claims.claim: Most of the random recombination in untreated MrgprdCreERT2; RosaiAP mice likely occurs postnatally.
claims.source: We noticed that most of this random recombination likely occurs postnatally, as untreated MrgprdCreERT2; RosaiAP tissue at P7 or younger shows no AP+ neurons (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of AP+ neurons at P7 or younger.

claims.claim: The temporal delay of recombination and the higher number of Mrgprd+ than Mrgpra/b/c+ neurons likely contribute to the specificity of sparse AP labeling.
claims.source: This temporal delay of recombination, along with the fact that there are many more Mrgprd+ than Mrgpra/b/c+ neurons (Liu et al., 2008; Dong et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2007), likely contributes to the specificity of sparse AP labeling in these mice.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the timing of recombination and relative population sizes, supported by citations.

claims.claim: A previous study suggested bushy ending terminals might correspond to C-fiber nociceptors or thermoceptors.
claims.source: In the periphery, sparse tracing of Pou4f1 expressing somatosensory neurons (which includes almost all somatosensory DRG neuron classes [Badea et al., 2012]) in the back hairy revealed a 'bushy ending' morphological type (Wu et al., 2012). The authors suggested these terminals might correspond to C-fiber nociceptors or thermoceptors.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous work supported by citations to Wu et al. 2012 and Badea et al. 2012.

claims.claim: Mrgprb4+ and TH+ C fibers mainly mediate light touch but not pain and innervate hairy skin only.
claims.source: In addition, Mrgprb4+ and TH+ C fibers, which mainly mediate light touch but not pain, and innervate hairy skin only, have been genetically traced and analyzed (Li et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Li et al. 2011 and Liu et al. 2007.

claims.claim: Mrgprb4+ neurons innervate the skin in large patches of free terminals.
claims.source: Mrgprb4+ neurons innervate the skin in large patches of free terminals (Liu et al., 2007)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al. 2007.

claims.claim: TH+ neurons form lanceolate endings around hair follicles.
claims.source: while TH+ neurons form lanceolate endings around hair follicles (Li et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al. 2011.

claims.claim: Single-cell tracing has not previously been performed for any C-fiber nociceptors innervating the glabrous skin.
claims.source: To our knowledge, single-cell tracing has not previously been performed for any C-fiber nociceptors innervating the glabrous skin.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current work based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claims.claim: Mrgprd+ nociceptors innervate both hairy and glabrous skin but not deep tissues.
claims.source: Mrgprd+ nociceptors innervate both hairy and glabrous skin but not deep tissues (Zylka et al., 2005)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Zylka et al. 2005.

claims.claim: A single Mrgprd+ afferent may signal both hair pulling as well as mechanical noxious stimuli applied to the skin surface.
claims.source: Our single-cell tracing suggests that a single Mrgprd+ afferent may signal both hair pulling as well as mechanical noxious stimuli applied to the skin surface. Further analysis would be required to test this possibility.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that single Mrgprd+ afferents innervate both hair follicles and interfollicular skin.

claims.claim: A previous study found smaller receptive fields in the distal leg for human mechanically responsive C-fiber units.
claims.source: This last result contrasts with an earlier study that performed single-fiber recordings of human mechanically responsive C-fiber units, which saw smaller receptive fields in the distal leg (Schmidt et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous work supported by citation to Schmidt et al. 1997.

claims.claim: The discrepancy between the current study and Schmidt et al. 1997 could be caused by differences between species, techniques, or the composition of neurons analyzed.
claims.source: This discrepancy could be caused by differences between species, techniques (physiological vs. direct anatomic tracing), or the composition of neurons that were analyzed (the previous study presumably recorded from multiple molecular classes).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about possible reasons for the discrepancy with previous work.

claims.claim: Classic studies described C-fiber afferent central arbors as longitudinally-oriented 'thin sheets' that are short in the mediolateral axis and extended in the rostrocadual axis.
claims.source: Classic studies have characterized the single-cell central arbors of C-fiber afferents using Golgi staining or backfill techniques and described them as longitudinally-oriented 'thin sheets' that are short in the mediolateral axis and extended in the rostrocadual axis (Sugiura et al., 1986; Sugiura et al., 1989; Scheibel and Scheibel, 1968).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous work supported by citations to Sugiura et al. 1986, 1989 and Scheibel and Scheibel 1968.

claims.claim: The classic description of C-fiber central arbors corresponds well to the 'long arbors' found in DH zones representing proximal limb and trunk regions.
claims.source: This description corresponds well to the 'long arbors' we found in DH zones representing proximal limb and trunk regions (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and previous literature.

claims.claim: The central terminals of Mrgprb4+ and TH+ C-fiber light touch neurons match the long terminal morphology.
claims.source: The central terminals of Mrgprb4+ and TH+ C-fiber light touch neurons also match this long terminal morphology, consistent with the fact that these classes only innervate hairy skin (Li et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citations to Li et al. 2011 and Liu et al. 2007.

claims.claim: A systematic comparison of nociceptive central terminals across the entire somatotopic map has not been conducted.
claims.source: Nevertheless, a systematic comparison of nociceptive central terminals across the entire somatotopic map has not been conducted.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current work based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claims.claim: The morphological difference between round and long arbors does not correlate with hairy vs. glabrous skin regions but instead seems to correlate with regions located at the extremities.
claims.source: Given that neurons in the medulla and sacral spinal cord display round arbors (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), this morphological difference does not correlate with hairy vs. glabrous skin regions but instead seems to correlate with regions located at the extremities.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of round arbors shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Region-specific central arbor structure could be a key contributor to the increased pain signal transmission of paw circuits.
claims.source: While we cannot rule out a role for regional differences in the single-cell physiology of Mrgprd+ neurons (such activation threshold, transmitter release, etc.), this correlation suggests that region-specific central arbor structure could be a key contributor to the increased pain signal transmission of paw circuits.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between arbor morphology and physiological responses.

claims.claim: Previous psychophysical studies that defined the 'pain fovea' in humans used heat nociceptive stimuli.
claims.source: Previous psychophysical studies that defined the 'pain fovea' in humans used heat nociceptive stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about previous human studies.

claims.claim: Thermal pain in mice is primarily mediated through CGRP+ peptidergic nociceptors.
claims.source: Thermal pain in mice is primarily mediated through a separate population of afferents (CGRP+ peptidergic nociceptors) from the Mrgprd+ fibers that we studied (Cavanaugh et al., 2009; McCoy et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cavanaugh et al. 2009 and McCoy et al. 2012.

results.result: Postnatal (P10-P17) tamoxifen treatment of MrgprdCreERT2 mice specifically labels Mrgprd+ non-peptidergic nociceptors with high efficiency (88.1±1% of ChR2-EYFP+ neurons express Mrgprd, 92.9±4.6% of Mrgprd+ neurons are labeled), while early embryonic treatment labels both Mrgprd+ and other Mrgpr+ neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C33 collectively demonstrate the temporal specificity of the MrgprdCreERT2 line through in situ hybridization and immunostaining data (Figure 1). The quantitative overlap data strongly support that postnatal tamoxifen treatment achieves specific and efficient labeling of Mrgprd+ neurons, while embryonic treatment is less specific due to broader developmental Mrgprd expression.

results.result: Untreated MrgprdCreERT2; RosaiAP mice show sparse background recombination labeling 3-11 neurons/DRG (<1% of total Mrgprd+ population), and 93.7±2.3% of these sparsely labeled neurons co-express Mrgprd markers, confirming specificity for adult Mrgprd+ nociceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 demonstrate that background recombination in untreated mice is both sparse and specific through AP staining, marker co-expression analysis, and triple transgenic validation (Figure 2). The quantitative data on labeling density and marker overlap strongly support the utility of this approach for single-cell tracing.

results.result: Mouse plantar paw skin has lower Mrgprd+ nociceptor density (21.0±3.0 cells/mm²) compared to proximal hindlimb (97.6±33.4 cells/mm²), but individual arbor sizes are comparable across regions (0.08-0.9 mm²). Peripheral arbors display 'bushy ending' morphology (98.4%) with regional variations in terminal structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C23, C39-C45 are well-supported by sparse genetic tracing (Figure 3), retrograde DiI labeling (Figure 3I, supplement 2), and morphological analysis. The quantitative measurements of neuron density, arbor size, and morphological classifications provide strong anatomical evidence. Statistical significance is reported for density differences (p=0.04).

results.result: Mrgprd+ nociceptor central arbors display two distinct morphologies: 'round' arbors (W/H ratio >0.2) in regions representing distal limbs, tail, anogenital, and head/face skin, and 'long' arbors (W/H ratio <0.2) in regions representing proximal limbs and trunk. These morphologies occupy mutually exclusive zones and correlate with peripheral innervation patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C51-C59 are strongly supported by systematic AP staining across the entire spinal cord (Figure 4, Figure 5), morphometric analysis, and correlation with established somatotopic maps. The dose-response experiment (Figure 5) confirms that segregation is maintained with increased labeling density, ruling out sampling artifacts. The correlation between peripheral and central arbor counts (Figure 4I) provides additional validation.

results.result: Peripheral and central arbors of neighboring Mrgprd+ nociceptors extensively overlap rather than tile, with multiple neurons innervating single hair follicles and overlapping territories in both skin and dorsal horn.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by dual-labeling experiments using MrgprdCreERT2/EGFPf; RosatdTomato mice (Figure 6), which directly visualize sparse labeled neurons within the context of the full population. The consistent co-innervation observed in both peripheral and central compartments provides strong evidence against tiling.

results.result: Plantar paw circuits show heightened signal transmission compared to trunk circuits. In ChR2 heterozygous mice, medial lumbar DH neurons show ~9-fold higher incidence of monosynaptic EPSCs (88.2% vs 10.5%) and lower pulse duration thresholds compared to lateral lumbar and thoracic neurons, despite comparable ChR2 expression levels and similar connectivity in homozygous mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C24-C25, C63-C70 are supported by systematic electrophysiology experiments (Figure 7) using both homozygous and heterozygous ChR2 mice. The use of heterozygous mice to reveal regional differences is well-justified by Western blot data showing ~40% ChR2 reduction. The comparable ChR2 expression across DRG regions (Figure 7 supplement 1) controls for expression-level confounds. The correlation between arbor morphology and physiological responses is compelling.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of Mrgprd+ nociceptors in behaving mice requires significantly lower light intensity to elicit withdrawal responses in paw (5 mW) compared to upper thigh (10-20 mW), despite higher neurite density and more superficial termination in leg skin.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C71-C79 are supported by systematic behavioral experiments with appropriate controls (Figure 8, videos). The anatomical characterization of neurite density and depth (Figure 8 supplement 1) strengthens the interpretation that behavioral differences reflect central rather than peripheral mechanisms. Statistical significance is reported (Chi-square test, p<0.001). The temporal delay analysis (Figure 8H) provides additional quantitative support.

results.result: The wider mediolateral spread of plantar paw nociceptor central arbors could facilitate 'afferent magnification' in downstream CNS circuits. The peripheral neurite density distribution and heightened distal limb pain sensitivity in mice are consistent with human findings, suggesting conserved organizational mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 represent interpretive conclusions and cross-species comparisons. While the correlation between arbor morphology and heightened sensitivity is well-demonstrated (C6, C26), the mechanistic claim about 'afferent magnification' (C80) remains speculative without direct evidence of downstream circuit organization. The comparison to human data (C81-C82) is reasonable but limited by differences in experimental approaches between studies.

results.result: Most Mrgprd+ central branches do not bifurcate (65.8%) and terminate within the segment of entry (72.6%), though some bifurcate (34.2%) or travel up to 3 segments (27.3%). Most neurons have one central arbor (91.9%), with few having 2-3 arbors.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 provide detailed quantitative characterization of central projection patterns based on AP staining of 234 neurons from 3 animals (Table 1). The sample size is adequate for these descriptive statistics, and the data are clearly presented.

results.result: Human distal limbs show high spatial acuity for noxious stimuli despite low density of pain-sensing neurites, suggesting region-specific organization exists in central pain circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C13 summarize established findings from human psychophysical and anatomical studies (Mancini et al. 2012, 2013, 2014) that motivate the current work. These are appropriately cited background claims that set up the research question.

results.result: High innervation density and smaller receptive field sizes of Aβ mechanoreceptors in primate distal limbs facilitate high spatial acuity for touch sensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 summarize well-established findings about the touch system from multiple cited studies. These provide important context for understanding regional specialization in somatosensation.

results.result: Mrgprd+ nociceptors mediate mechanical pain and beta-alanine triggered itch, are the most abundant cutaneous polymodal C-fiber nociceptors, and likely correspond to PGP9.5+ terminals in human skin biopsies.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 summarize established functional and anatomical properties of Mrgprd+ neurons from prior literature (Cavanaugh et al. 2009, Liu et al. 2012, Zylka et al. 2005, Mancini et al. 2013). The comparison to human PGP9.5+ terminals (C22) is appropriately qualified as 'likely' given the indirect nature of the comparison.

results.result: Adult mice have two functionally distinct Mrgpr+ DRG populations, with Mrgpra/b/c+ neurons transiently expressing Mrgprd during early development. Background recombination in MrgprdCreERT2 mice likely occurs postnatally, contributing to labeling specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 provide important context about Mrgpr expression patterns and explain the temporal specificity of the MrgprdCreERT2 line. C85-C86 involve some inference from negative data (no AP+ neurons at P7), but the reasoning is sound and supported by the broader expression pattern literature.

results.result: Nociceptors are pseudounipolar neurons with cell bodies in DRG/TG and bifurcating axons terminating in skin peripherally and dorsal horn centrally. Previous studies have not established a comprehensive model of mammalian pain system somatotopic organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 state basic anatomical facts about nociceptor organization. C18 provides a fair critique of prior literature, noting that while individual studies have traced nociceptors, systematic somatotopic comparisons were lacking.

results.result: Previous studies have characterized peripheral terminals of various somatosensory neuron types, but systematic single-cell tracing of C-fiber nociceptors innervating glabrous skin had not been performed.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 accurately summarize prior work on somatosensory neuron tracing and identify a gap in the literature that the current study addresses. The citations are appropriate and the characterization of prior work appears accurate.

results.result: Single Mrgprd+ afferents may signal both hair pulling and mechanical noxious stimuli to skin surface, though this requires further testing. Discrepancies with a previous human study finding smaller distal receptive fields could reflect species, technical, or neuronal population differences.
results.evaluation: C93 is appropriately qualified as speculation requiring further analysis. C94-C95 acknowledge a discrepancy with Schmidt et al. 1997 and offer reasonable explanations, but the discrepancy remains unresolved. These represent honest acknowledgment of limitations and alternative interpretations.

results.result: Classic studies described C-fiber central arbors as longitudinally-oriented 'thin sheets,' corresponding to the 'long arbors' found in trunk regions. The morphological difference correlates with extremity vs. trunk location rather than hairy vs. glabrous skin.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 appropriately contextualize the current findings within prior literature and make reasonable inferences about the anatomical correlates of arbor morphology based on the distribution data (Figure 4, Figure 4 supplement 1C).

results.result: Region-specific central arbor structure could be a key contributor to increased pain signal transmission in paw circuits, though regional differences in single-cell physiology cannot be ruled out.
results.evaluation: C101 represents a mechanistic interpretation that is well-supported by the correlation between arbor morphology and physiological responses, but remains somewhat speculative without direct manipulation of arbor structure or more detailed analysis of synaptic properties. The acknowledgment of alternative explanations is appropriate.

results.result: Human 'pain fovea' studies used heat stimuli, which are primarily mediated by CGRP+ peptidergic nociceptors in mice rather than Mrgprd+ neurons. Whether peptidergic fibers show similar somatotopic central arbor differences remains unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 appropriately acknowledge a limitation in directly comparing the current findings to human psychophysical studies, as different nociceptor populations may be involved. This represents honest discussion of the scope and limitations of the work.

results.result: Previous studies suggest Aβ mechanoreceptor DH collaterals are wider in medial lumbar enlargement, but it is unclear whether this contributes to differential touch sensitivity since primary signal transmission occurs in dorsal column nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 accurately summarize prior work on Aβ mechanoreceptors and appropriately note the uncertainty about functional significance given the different anatomical organization of the touch system.

results.result: DH layer II interneurons are heterogeneous, and Mrgprd+ fibers synapse on most classes and signal to projection neurons through polysynaptic pathways. Whether systematic somatotopic differences exist in DH interneuron circuit organization is unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 accurately summarize established knowledge about DH circuits and identify an important gap for future research. The acknowledgment of uncertainty about somatotopic differences in interneuron organization is appropriate.

results.result: Peripheral optogenetic stimulation likely bypasses some peripheral parameters affecting natural stimuli sensation. The laser stimulus is unlikely to have preferential access to paw terminals given their deeper location, though other unmeasured regional differences cannot be ruled out.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 provide thoughtful discussion of the advantages and limitations of the optogenetic approach. The reasoning about depth of termination (C114) is supported by anatomical data (Figure 8 supplement 1). The acknowledgment of potential unmeasured factors (C115) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Pain research has historically focused on plantar paw/medial lumbar circuits. Examining region-specific differences in pain model pathways could inform translation of preclinical findings to clinical treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 appropriately discuss the implications of the findings for pain research methodology and suggest reasonable directions for future work. These represent thoughtful consideration of the broader impact of the findings.
